stories.title: US-Israel war on Iran, six months down the line: In numbers
stories.summary: Al Jazeera tracks six months of the Iran war, from the dead and displaced to the shock delivered to the global economy. Six months ago today, the United States and Israel launched their first strikes of on Iran, assassinating Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei in Tehran and hitting nuclear and military sites around the country. Those attacks prompted Iran to begin strikes on US military assets and infrastructure in Gulf countries – and for the Lebanese armed group, Hezbollah, to fire rockets into northern Israel, prompting near-daily Israeli responses since then and, at one point, control over one-fifth of Lebanon. Neither side has gained the upper hand since. Iran has used its control of the Strait of Hormuz to squeeze Washington and global energy markets, and the conflict has settled into a stalemate, which months of negotiation have not broken. Al Jazeera tracks the first six months of the war, from the numbers killed and displaced to the shock suffered by the global economy. According to the latest official figures, at least 4,350 people are confirmed killed in Lebanon, 3,527 in Iran and 28 in Gulf states since the war began on February 28. A further 60 Israelis and 18 US service members have been killed in Iranian attacks. The Pentagon says 757 US personnel have been wounded. Figures are compiled from national health ministries and official bodies, and may change as the situation evolves and more information becomes available. According to the Armed Conflict Location and Event Data project (ACLED), a US-based conflict monitoring group, the US and Israel have carried out at least 3,580 attacks on Iran since February 28. Over the same period, Iran carried out at least 2,053 attacks across the Gulf and the wider Middle East.

stories.title: India: Citizen-led school audits test the limits of activism
stories.summary: The Indian activist movement dubbing itself the "Cockroach Janta Party (CJP)" shot to national prominence in May by leading weeks-long protests over a scandal involving highly competitive entrance exams. The student-led campaign put the government under intense political pressure and ended with the resignation of Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan last month. Now, the CJP is taking aim at India's government schools, organizing volunteers visiting classrooms, documenting conditions and demanding accountability for problems. Launched on August 15, India's Independence Day, the campaign asks parents, students and volunteers to inspect schools and record basic facilities including toilets, drinking water, electricity, classroom furniture and school buildings. The CJP says the findings will be used to pressure authorities to make improvements. Its initial target is to audit 100 rural government schools over two months. It has also proposed giving recognition to village leaders who improve their schools. Unlike the first campaign, which was based on street protests, the school audits require a more sustained form of local activism. Volunteers are expected to work consistently at the local level, document conditions and follow up with officials, parents and communities. The organization is dealing with different layers of the Indian administration. Responsibility for government schools is divided between state governments, local administrations and elected village bodies. The CJP is therefore set to tackle different rules and political interests across the country.

stories.title: South Korea leans toward military conscription for women
stories.summary: Nearly 60% of South Koreans are now in favor of young women serving mandatory military service alongside their male counterparts, according to a recent survey, representing a significant shift in the long-held taboo against women being obliged to defend the nation. Thousands of women already serve in the South Korean armed forces on a voluntary basis, but the debate over mandatory service has always been delicate. Now, for a series of reasons that include a falling birth rate and shrinking number of recruits as well as an insistence that social equality means that women should also serve, the issue has re-emerged ahead of a reform of the national defense plan scheduled to be released this autumn. Yet, there are still those who insist that women should be kept away from the front lines and, instead, that South Korea should invest more in drones and other advanced technologies. "South Korea's male-centered conscription system has long been closely connected to traditional gender roles," said Hyobin Lee, a professor at Sogang University in Seoul. "Men were generally expected to protect the country and the family and to fight in wartime, while women were expected to take primary responsibility for childbirth, childcare and the household," she told DW. A second factor is the intensifying debate about gender equality, a debate in large part driven by young men, she said. "South Korean men generally perform their military service in their early 20s, which interrupts their education, employment or early career development," Lee said. "At the same time, gender equality has become an increasingly important social value, and women's opportunities in education and employment have expanded." "As a result, some younger men ask a very simple question: If society expects equality in rights and opportunities, why does one of the country's most significant civic obligations – military service – still fall only on men?" Another contributing factor is the change in the nature of the military itself, with a shift away from physically demanding combat roles that were perceived as being more suited to men and the emergence of a national defense more heavily reliant on technology. This includes unmanned systems, cyber capabilities, information and communications technology and others that do not require physical strength.
